BBC

NHS consultant warns of roadside births risk

The inspection of maternity services in Dumfries was carried out earlier this year

A baby's feet and toes pictured in close-up being held in an adult's hand

The risk of babies being born by the roadside would increase if maternity units at two hospitals in Norfolk were closed, a senior obstetrician has warned.

Alastair McKelvey said he was \"worried\" about the possibility of cuts at the Queen Elizabeth Hospital in King's Lynn and James Paget Hospital in Gorleston.

The Norfolk and Waveney University Hospitals Group (NWUHG) has set out proposals on how services could be changed, but has stressed that no decisions have yet been made.

One possibility put forward is to move all births to the county's largest hospital, the Norfolk and Norwich (N&N).

McKelvey, who is a consultant at the N&N and also sits on the council of the Royal College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists (RCOG), said staff across all three hospitals had concerns about the distances that women would have to travel to give birth.

The Queen Elizabeth is just over 40 miles away from the Norwich hospital, while the James Paget is 29 miles away.

McKelvey said clinicians were \"particularly anxious\" about the impact any closures would have on women from poorer backgrounds who were more likely to rely on public transport to get to hospital.

\"We are worried that closure of either unit would also lead to an increase in unplanned out of hospital births, for example by the roadside or in ambulances,\" he explained.

NWUHG's Lesley Dwyer repeatedly told a council meeting that no decisions had been made on the future of the hospitals

As part of its proposals, NWUHG published a document setting out its \"case for change\".

McKelvey said he was pleased the report acknowledged births were becoming more complex, with caesarean section rates rising, hospital buildings in need of improvement and ongoing staffing challenges.

But he said the focus should be on improving all three maternity units, rather than closing any of them.

Councillor Lucy Shires said NWUHG needed to \"do better\" at being transparent about its plans

His comments came as NWUHG bosses faced two hours of questions about their plans from councillors on Norfolk's Health Overview and Scrutiny committee.

At the meeting, chief nurse Rachael Cocker said she recognised \"maternity is one of the most sensitive areas for the case for change.\"

\"Just to be really clear no decision has to be made to close, reduce or relocate any of our maternity services at any of the three hospitals,\" she added.

But committee chair, Liberal Democrat Lucy Shires, said she was \"disappointed\" that NWUHG had \"decided there is a case for change rather than coming to us to discuss the challenges first\".

\"On behalf of Norfolk, I ask that you do better, \" she added.

The group's chief executive Lesley Dwyer insisted no decisions had been made but said there was \"enough evidence\" to continue investigating potential changes.

She said: \"There is a lengthy process ahead including more detailed analysis, engagement with patients, with our staff [and] consideration of different options.\"

However, she conceded that in the future \"as far as what we share, we have to now be much more transparent.\"
